**[Question 1] - What is the problem?**

Can a privacy-calibrated, reliability-gated personalized federated distillation method use differentially private synthetic replay to improve worst-client accuracy and calibration under simultaneous Non-IID data, class imbalance, domain shift, noisy labels, and low-quality inputs?

**[Question 2] - Why is it interesting and important?**

Current personalized federated learning methods primarily optimize average predictive performance under statistical heterogeneity. A method that also protects private information, handles unreliable local data, and improves minority-client performance would advance personalized FL toward trustworthy deployment in healthcare, mobile sensing, and financial applications.

The key scientific contribution would be a unified privacy–utility–fairness framework. It could shift evaluation beyond global accuracy toward worst-client accuracy, calibration, privacy guarantees, and robustness. This would provide a foundation for future research on reliable knowledge transfer when clients have missing classes, scarce data, or systematically different acquisition conditions.

**[Question 3] - Why is it hard?**

A global teacher may be poorly calibrated for a particular client and transfer harmful domain-specific features. Confidence filtering alone is insufficient: a correctly labeled low-quality image may be uncertain, while a mislabeled image may receive high confidence.

Differential privacy further complicates the problem because noise disproportionately damages rare classes and small clients. A generator trained from privatized statistics may produce inaccurate or memorized samples, while synthetic replay can amplify teacher bias. In addition, prototypes, feature statistics, and model updates can leak information unless they are clipped, privatized, and evaluated against inference attacks.

The method must therefore simultaneously control negative transfer, noisy supervision, privacy degradation, communication cost, and computational overhead.

**[Question 4] - Why hasn’t it been solved before?**

FedAvg learns one global model and often performs poorly under heterogeneous data. FedProx improves optimization stability, while pFedMe and pFedHN personalize models through regularization or hypernetworks; however, these approaches generally assume that local labels and transferred knowledge are reliable.

Distillation methods such as MOON transfer representations but can impose a mismatched global teacher. Generative FL methods such as FedGen address missing or imbalanced classes but generally do not combine synthetic replay with formal privacy accounting and reliability-aware personalization. Differentially private FL protects updates but often treats all clients similarly, causing excessive utility loss for minority clients.

The proposed approach differs by combining client-specific adapters, uncertainty- and domain-aware distillation gates, and a replay generator trained only from differentially private latent statistics. It explicitly evaluates both formal privacy and practical leakage, rather than assuming that federated training alone provides sufficient protection.

**[Question 5] - What are the key components of my approach and results?**

The proposed method, **Privacy-Calibrated Reliability-Gated Personalized Federated Distillation (PCRG-pFL)**, will include:

1. A globally aggregated encoder and teacher, plus a lightweight private adapter and classifier head retained by each client.

2. A reliability gate based on teacher entropy, prediction consistency under augmentations, teacher–student disagreement, and distance to global class prototypes. Distillation will be weakened when the teacher is uncertain or mismatched to the client domain.

3. A robust local objective combining generalized or symmetric cross-entropy, gated logit distillation, feature alignment, and personalized adapter training.

4. Differentially private, clipped class-conditional latent statistics uploaded through secure aggregation. A lightweight conditional latent generator will be trained only from these privatized statistics and will provide class-balanced synthetic replay for clients with missing or underrepresented classes. Privacy will be tracked using an RDP accountant with explicit \((\varepsilon,\delta)\) guarantees.

5. Experiments on CIFAR-100 with Dirichlet label skew, quantity imbalance, missing classes, 20–60% label noise, and blur/compression corruptions; FEMNIST for naturally heterogeneous clients; and Office-Home or PACS for domain-shift evaluation.

6. Comparisons against FedAvg, FedProx, pFedMe, pFedHN, Ditto, FedRep, MOON, FedGen, DP-FedAvg, and robust noisy-label FL methods.

Evaluation will report mean accuracy, worst-client and 10th-percentile accuracy, macro-F1, minority-class recall, calibration error, Brier score, clean-to-corrupted performance drop, communication volume, client computation, synthetic-data utility, formal privacy budgets, membership-inference success, and reconstruction leakage. Ablations will remove the reliability gate, private replay, personalization, and adaptive privacy mechanism.

The expected result is improved worst-client performance and calibration at a fixed privacy budget, especially for clients with scarce data or missing classes, with graceful degradation as privacy becomes stricter and modest communication overhead.
